description:
We are Team sphot, six students from Sungkyunkwan University, South Korea. We share a curiosity about space and a love of building things people can use.

Our skills:

Data analysis: real SPHEREx data

Backend design: sky patches on demand

Frontend development: web app and 3D sky

UI/UX design: simple, fun labeling

Our goal is to make NASA’s open SPHEREx data easy and fun for anyone to explore, so volunteers can spot what moved and help find new objects.
summary:
Billions of dots fill the sky, and a few of them are on the move.

SPHEREx, a NASA space telescope, is the first to map the whole sky in 102 infrared colors, light that human eyes cannot see. Its images hold billions of objects, and the most direct clue to an unknown one is movement. Citizen science volunteers have long searched for such movement by eye.

That work is hard to keep up. Volunteers flip through many images without knowing whether anything moved at all, and their eyes tire. SPHEREx data also starts with sky coordinates, which are hard to choose without background knowledge, and its targets are open: any object bright in the infrared is worth a look.

We decided that labeling should be fun, and that complex data should be preprocessed before it reaches the user, in a form that is easy to view. So we built ‘sphot’, a web tool that visualizes SPHEREx data.

With ‘sphot’, volunteers enjoy the search and feel a bond with others. Because many people label the same images, ‘sphot’ also supports ensemble validation, cross-checking labels from many volunteers. Every answer stays as open data that can help narrow down the next candidates.

Lie back, look up, and spot what moved.
details:
sphot: spot what moved in the SPHEREx sky.

‘sphot’ is a web tool that lets anyone look for moving objects in SPHEREx images. You pick a spot on the sky, ‘sphot’ lines up the visits that are fair to compare, and you answer whether something moved. Every answer becomes an open label that others can check against the same images.

How it works

Telescope: Look up & Spot.

Users drift across the SPHEREx all-sky map, as if lying back under the night sky, and zoom into a point. The point they choose becomes the coordinates, so nobody has to type them. ‘Mono’, our mascot, explains each screen in English or Korean.

Studio: Explore & Answer.

- For Everyone

‘sphot’ prepares that patch of sky on the server and plays the visits in time order. Users can flip through frames, overlay them, or view the difference between two of them. Two clicks, one on the first visit and one on the last, show how far an object moved in arcseconds and months. Users then answer moved, blinks, stayed, or can't tell, before seeing anyone else's answer, and answers are final.

- For Experts

Click the ‘Details' button on the Studio page to view the exact metadata values and features of each band. We also converted this information into a blackbody radiation graph, so that you can compare it with the spectra of several well-known molecules.

Board: Discuss.

After answering, users see how others labelled the same spot and can browse other spots on the board. A spot becomes a Hot 'sphot' when at least five independent users answer and 70% or more agree. When agreement falls between 30% and 70%, it is marked Needs eyes and asks for more people to look.

New users start with practice cards that have known answers. All labels are exported as an open dataset without nicknames (CC BY 4.0), together with the images they were based on. On every screen, ‘sphot’ keeps apart what SPHEREx observed, what a catalogue predicts, and what the user decided.

Data pipeline

We used SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 single exposures from NASA/IPAC IRSA, the SPHEREx all-sky map for the sky background, and Gaia DR3. SIMBAD is used to look up names of known objects. All images are placed on the same sky grid, and only frames that are fair to compare are shown together.

We also examined WISE and NEOSSat images, but their dates, brightness, and resolution differ from SPHEREx, so the main view shows SPHEREx only. They are still useful for checking: of the 37 asteroids and comets NEOSSat imaged during the SPHEREx mission, 33 also appear in SPHEREx frames, including the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, which both telescopes imaged on the same day.

Validation with the five challenge targets

  • Epsilon Indi B: It moved 6.3″ (about one pixel) in 17 months. The move is clear in the sequence and matches the catalog prediction.
  • WISE 0855−0714: It is cold, faint, and fast. It is weak in single frames but visible after stacking. The challenge coordinates are 127″ from its current position, so 'sphot' follows its catalog path to open the right patch.
  • Barnard’s Star: It is saturated in 357 of 358 exposures. 'sphot' explains this and offers only “unclear”. The catalog path still tracks where the star is.
  • RW Aurigae: It is mostly saturated (9 of 335 exposures are comparable). It shows no motion, and 'sphot' shows its brightness change as a chart.
  • R Draconis: It is saturated in every exposure, so positions cannot be compared. Its brightness change is read from the outer ring of the star as a relative value.

User test

We shared one link and asked 90 people to try ‘sphot’ on their phones or laptop. 90 people joined and left 300 labels. Everyone got the same first card, Epsilon Indi B, and 100% answered “moved”, which is the right answer. Of the 90 testers, 90% said exploring ‘sphot’ felt like a fun journey through the night sky. This supports our main UX choice: starting from the sky itself instead of a coordinate box. Before the test, we checked the server with 100 simulated visitors at the same time: 3,994 requests, 95% answered within 235 ms, and no errors.

Also, the team opens an admin page with a private key. It shows real numbers in one place: how many people joined, how many labels they left, and how everyone answered the same first card. The labels can be downloaded as CSV files, so the next research step can start from what volunteers actually saw.

Mascot, 'Mono'

Astronomy can feel closed to newcomers: unfamiliar coordinates, file formats, and terms stand between a curious volunteer and the sky. We made Mono, our mascot, to be the bridge across that gap. Mono walks first-time users through ‘sphot’ in short, friendly lines, in English or Korean. In the opening, Mono shows where the first star sits on the sky and explains that SPHEREx photographs it again every six months, so two visits can be compared. In the studio, Mono runs a short tour of the controls, and after each answer it shows what was measured, such as how far the star moved and over how many months. Mono never treats a wrong answer as a failure, and it never answers for the user: the label is always the user's own decision.

Tools

Python (FastAPI, Astropy) for data preparation and the API. React, TypeScript, and three.js for the web app. Deployed on Fly.io with Docker.

‘sphot’ turns a hard archive search into a short judgment that anyone can make and others can check.

Appendix

Flowchart of ‘sphot’

URL for each web view

https://sphot.fly.dev — Flip through real SPHEREx infrared photos from NASA and spot stars that moved or blinked; your answers become open data for researchers.

https://sphot.fly.dev/go — A one-minute guided start with Mono: spot your first moving star and get your own sky report.

https://sphot.fly.dev/film — Our 30-second film: how 'sphot' turns SPHEREx data and many people's eyes into open labels.

https://sphot.fly.dev/telescope — Point your phone at the real sky (or pair it with a laptop) to see SPHEREx candidates and 'Hot sphots' right where they are above you.
